questions.question: What is the String pool in Java?
questions.title: What Is the String Pool in Java?
questions.direct_answer: The string pool is the JVM's canonical set of interned strings. String literals and compile-time constant string expressions are interned, and `String.intern()` returns the canonical object for equal content. Pooled strings are ordinary String objects managed in the heap in modern HotSpot; do not use `==` as a content test even though equal interned references are identical.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand where string literals live in memory and why the JVM can safely share them.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking all Strings go into the pool. Only literals and interned strings go there. `new String('hello')` is not itself automatically interned and always creates a new heap object.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that the pool is only safe because Strings are immutable — if one variable could modify 'hello', every other variable pointing to the same pooled object would be corrupted. Immutability and the pool are inseparable.

sections.title: One Copy of Each Literal, Shared Across the Program
sections.content:
The **string pool** keeps a canonical String object for each interned value. Java requires identical string literals and compile-time constant string expressions to refer to the same interned instance. Calling `intern()` on a runtime-created string returns the canonical instance with equal content, adding one if needed.

This can reduce duplicate objects for commonly repeated constant text. It also explains why `"hello" == "hello"` is true: both operands denote the same interned object. That identity is guaranteed for interned constant strings, but ordinary runtime strings are not automatically interned.

Use `equals()` for content regardless of origin. Whether a value came from a file, concatenation, or `new String` should not change program correctness. In modern HotSpot, pooled strings are ordinary heap objects; the pool is a logical interning mechanism, not a separate Java-language memory area.

sections.title: Literal vs new String() — Pool vs Heap
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    L["literal or constant expression: hello"] --> P["canonical interned String: hello"]
    R["runtime String with content hello"] --> I["runtime.intern()"]
    I --> P
    N["new String(hello)"] --> O["fresh, non-interned String object"]
    O -. "equals is true; identity differs" .-> P
```

sections.title: Pool Sharing vs new String — the == Difference
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking every `String` lives in the pool** — literals, compile-time constant string expressions, and strings represented canonically through `intern()` are pooled; `new String("hello")`, concatenation results, and strings from input or files land on the regular heap.
- **Comparing content with `==`** — `==` checks whether two references point to the same object, not whether the characters match; it returns `true` for two literals by luck of pooling and `false` for a `new String`. Use `.equals()`.
- **Assuming `new String("hello")` holds different text** — the content is identical to the literal; only the object identity differs, which is exactly why `==` and `.equals()` disagree.
- **Believing the pool still lives in PermGen** — since Java 7 it sits in the normal heap, so pooled strings are subject to garbage collection like any other object.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Pool**: canonical objects for interned string values.
- **Automatic**: literals and compile-time constant string expressions are interned.
- **Manual**: `intern()` returns the canonical equal string.
- **Identity effect**: equal interned strings use the same object.
- **Correct comparison**: use `equals()` for content; never depend on pooling in business logic.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The string pool stores a canonical object for each interned string value. Literals and compile-time constant string expressions are interned automatically, and `intern()` returns the canonical object for a runtime value. That is why two identical literals compare true with `==`.

I still use `equals()` for content, because input and most runtime-created strings are not automatically interned. The pool is an optimization and canonicalization mechanism; it should not decide whether an equality check works.

groups.text: A quoted literal goes through the pool. The String pool interns string literals, so two equal literals share one object.

groups.heading: New object

questions.question: What is the difference between `String s = "hello"` and `String s = new String("hello")` in Java?
questions.title: String Literal vs new String() in Java
questions.direct_answer: `String s = "hello"` uses the canonical interned literal. `new String("hello")` evaluates that literal and then creates a distinct String object with the same content; the new object is not automatically interned. Therefore `equals()` is true between them but `==` is false. The constructor is almost never needed for an existing String.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the memory and identity implications of using a literal vs constructor, and can explain why == gives different results in each case.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using == to compare a literal and a new String() and expecting true — they are different objects even if the content is identical.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that `new String('hello')` is almost never the right choice in production code — the only reason you'd use it is if you have a very long char array and want a String from a small slice of it, preventing the whole array from being retained in memory.

sections.title: Same Characters, Two Different Objects in Memory
sections.content:
A string literal such as `"hello"` denotes its canonical interned String object. Repeating that literal uses the same canonical object.

A class-instance creation expression, `new String("hello")`, must create a fresh String object. The argument literal still refers to the pooled object, but the newly constructed result is a separate, non-interned object with equal content. Therefore `literal.equals(created)` is true while `literal == created` is false.

This constructor does not provide a useful defensive copy because String is immutable. It is normally unnecessary. It also has nothing to do with slicing a large character array; constructors from arrays create a String from the supplied range, and modern String implementations do not retain an arbitrary caller-owned array as a mutable backing store.

sections.title: Literal vs new String()
sections.content:
| Expression | Result | Automatically interned? |
|---|---|---:|
| `String a = "hello"` | reference to canonical literal | Yes |
| `String b = "hello"` | same canonical literal as `a` | Yes |
| `String c = new String("hello")` | fresh object with equal content | No |

`a == b` is true, `a == c` is false, and `a.equals(c)` is true.

sections.title: Where Each One Lives: Pool vs Heap
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["a = literal hello"] --> P["canonical interned hello"]
    B["b = literal hello"] --> P
    C["c = new String(hello)"] --> N["fresh String object: hello"]
    N -. "same content, different identity" .-> P
```

sections.title: Proving the Memory Difference with ==
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting `==` to be `true` for a literal and a `new String`** — they hold the same characters but are different objects, so `==` is `false`; this is the single most common `String` bug for freshers.
- **Reaching for `new String("...")` to 'make a copy'** — it copies pointlessly; literals are already safe to share because `String` is immutable, so the copy buys you nothing but wasted memory.
- **Assuming strings from input, files, or concatenation are pooled** — only literals and explicitly `intern()`-ed strings live in the pool; a value read at runtime is a fresh heap object, so `==` against a literal fails.
- **Thinking `.equals()` and `==` are interchangeable** — `.equals()` compares characters and is what you almost always want; `==` compares object identity and happens to work for literals by accident.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Literal**: uses the canonical interned object.
- **`new String(literal)`**: creates a distinct String object with equal content.
- **The literal still uses the pool**; only the constructed result is not automatically interned.
- **`equals()`**: true for equal content; **`==`**: false for these two objects.
- **Normal choice**: use the literal or existing String directly; the copy constructor is rarely useful.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The literal form uses the canonical interned `hello` object. `new String("hello")` first evaluates that literal and then creates a separate String object with the same content. The new object is not automatically placed in the pool.

That gives `literal.equals(created) == true` but `literal == created == false`. In ordinary code the constructor adds no value because String is immutable, so I use the literal or existing String reference and compare text with `equals()`.

questions.question: What happens internally when you concatenate strings with the + operator in Java?
questions.title: How Java's + Operator Works for Strings
questions.direct_answer: String `+` is a language feature, not a guaranteed `StringBuilder` rewrite. Compile-time constant string expressions are folded and interned. For runtime concatenation, modern javac commonly emits `invokedynamic` and `StringConcatFactory`; the JVM chooses an efficient recipe. Repeatedly extending a growing String in a loop can still copy earlier text, so use one `StringBuilder` for that pattern.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that + on Strings is not a primitive operation — the compiler transforms it, but only in a limited way that can produce O(n²) behavior in loops.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming the compiler always uses one fixed StringBuilder translation, including inside loops. The compiler can only see single expressions — not loop iteration sequences.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that since Java 9, the JVM uses a more dynamic concatenation strategy via invokedynamic (StringConcatFactory) which can be even more efficient than a classic StringBuilder chain — but the key interview point is still: use StringBuilder explicitly in loops.

sections.title: Why `+` on Strings Quietly Becomes a StringBuilder — Until a Loop Ruins It
sections.content:
Java defines the result of string concatenation but leaves the implementation strategy to the compiler and JVM. A constant expression such as `"a" + "b"` is folded to the interned constant `"ab"`. When runtime values participate, current javac normally emits an `invokedynamic` concatenation call site, which the JVM can implement with a suitable recipe. Older compilers commonly emitted explicit `StringBuilder` calls.

This means 'every plus becomes a new StringBuilder' is outdated and not a language guarantee. It also means exact temporary-object counts should not be promised.

The practical performance issue remains: `result += part` in a loop repeatedly combines an ever-growing prefix. Use one builder outside the loop for predictable linear assembly. For a short readable expression outside a loop, use `+`.

sections.title: Single-Line + vs Loop + — What the Compiler Actually Produces
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["String concatenation"] --> C{"Compile-time constant?"}
    C -->|"yes"| F["fold to one constant String"]
    C -->|"no"| R["compiler emits runtime concatenation call site"]
    R --> J["JVM selects an implementation strategy"]
    L["Growing result inside loop"] --> B["Prefer one StringBuilder outside loop"]
```

sections.title: What the Compiler Does — and Where It Can't Help
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Believing the compiler optimises `+` inside loops** — it only rewrites a single expression; it cannot merge iterations, so `result = result + word` in a loop is genuinely O(n²), not the efficient `StringBuilder` chain people assume.
- **Using `String +=` to build large strings** — every `+=` allocates a new `StringBuilder` and a new `String`; for thousands of items this shows up as real CPU and GC pressure. Use one `StringBuilder`.
- **Calling `toString()` inside the loop** — even with a manual `StringBuilder`, materialising the string every iteration throws away the benefit; call `toString()` exactly once after the loop.
- **Assuming `StringBuffer` is the answer for performance** — `StringBuffer` is synchronized and slower; in single-threaded code (the common case) `StringBuilder` is the right choice.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Constant strings**: `"a" + "b"` is folded to `"ab"`.
- **Runtime strings**: modern javac usually uses `invokedynamic`/`StringConcatFactory`.
- **No fixed translation**: Java does not promise one StringBuilder per expression.
- **Loop warning**: repeatedly growing a String can recopy the prefix.
- **Use one builder** for repeated assembly; keep `+` for small expressions.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The `+` operator is Java's built-in string-concatenation syntax, but the language does not require one fixed implementation strategy. Constant expressions can be folded while compiling. For runtime values, current `javac` versions normally use `invokedynamic` concatenation machinery, while older bytecode explanations often show a generated `StringBuilder` chain.

For example, `String label = "User " + id;` is a clear one-line expression and should usually remain that way. By contrast, repeatedly doing `result = result + item` inside a loop creates a new immutable result at each step and repeatedly copies the growing content. A `StringBuilder` created before the loop, followed by `append(item)`, expresses that one mutable buffer is being accumulated. So I do not promise an exact object count for every plus expression; I choose between readable one-off concatenation and an explicit builder for repeated construction.
